q: When a DCF is valued partway through a year, what is the partial interval from the valuation date to year-end called?
explain: A stub period arises when the valuation date is not the start of a fiscal year; its discount period is the remaining days of the year divided by the total days in the year.
hook: A stub is the leftover piece of the year.

sources.title: Mid-Year Convention DCF and Mid-Year Discounting
sources.quote: This interval between April 30 and December 31 is called the stub period . To determine the discount period for this stub period , you take the remaining days of the year and divide by the total days in the year.

sources.title: Mid-Year Convention and Stub Periods in DCF — Knowledge Centre — Oxxon Advisors
sources.quote: A stub period arises whenever the valuation date does not fall exactly at the start of a fiscal year — for example, a valuation as of 1 April requires the first forecast "period" to cover only 1 April to 31 December of that year, nine months rather than a full twelve.

q: When combining a stub period with the mid-year convention, the first-year discount period equals the stub fraction divided by what?
explain: Cash flow is assumed to arrive midway between the valuation date and year-end; later periods use the normal discount period minus 0.5, not another halving.

sources.title: Mid-Year Convention DCF and Mid-Year Discounting
sources.quote: If you do this, the first discount period will be the stub period fraction divided by 2.

sources.title: How to Apply Mid-Year Convention and Stub Periods in Discounted Cash Flow Valuation Models | StableBread
sources.quote: In the first projected year (year 1), calculate the mid-year stub discount period by halving the stub discount period (0.252), resulting in 0.126 (0.252 / 2).

sources.title: Mid-Year Convention and Stub Periods in DCF — Knowledge Centre — Oxxon Advisors
sources.quote: Mid-year stub discount factor:    DF_stub = 1 / (1 + r)^(stub fraction / 2)
